```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = TRUE)

# Fold every code block into a collapsible <details> element. GitHub renders this
# natively, so the rendered document reads as a summary while the full code stays
# one click away.
knitr::knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options) {
  paste0("\n<details>\n<summary>Code</summary>\n\n``` r\n",
         paste(x, collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n\n</details>\n")
})

# All summary output goes through kable, with the caption as a bold line *above*
# the table - kable's own caption ends up below it, where it reads as a stray
# sentence on GitHub.
tab <- function(x, caption = NULL) {
  md <- paste(knitr::kable(x), collapse = "\n")
  if (!is.null(caption)) md <- paste0("**", caption, "**\n\n", md)
  knitr::asis_output(paste0("\n", md, "\n"))
}
```

Follow-up analysis on the annotated master table built in
[Master_Table.Rmd](Master_Table.Rmd) (see [its rendered output](Readme.md) for how
the annotation columns are defined). This document starts by reducing the table
to the genes that are actually worth looking at. Code blocks are collapsed -
click *Code* to expand.

```{r load_packages}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(patchwork)
library(openxlsx)

```


# Input

`master_counts_table.xlsx` carries everything: the DESeq2 contrasts, the
annotation columns, and the per-sample normalized counts. Reading 65 MB of Excel
on every knit is slow, so it is cached as an RDS and only re-read when the xlsx
is newer.

```{r load_master}

in_dir  <- here::here("6_XM_data_merge")
xlsx_in <- file.path(in_dir, "master_counts_table.xlsx")
rds_cache <- file.path(in_dir, "cache", "master_counts_table.rds")

dir.create(dirname(rds_cache), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
if (file.exists(rds_cache) &&
    file.mtime(rds_cache) > file.mtime(xlsx_in)) {
  master <- readRDS(rds_cache)
} else {
  master <- as.data.frame(readxl::read_xlsx(xlsx_in))
  saveRDS(master, rds_cache)
}

count_cols <- grep("^counts_", colnames(master), value = TRUE)

tab(data.frame(
  Item = c("genes", "columns", "of them per-sample counts", "annotation columns"),
  n    = c(nrow(master), ncol(master), length(count_cols),
           sum(colnames(master) %in% c("Target", "Hx_Baseline", "pubmed_total",
                                       "pubmed_hypoxia", "pubmed_source", "HR_risk")))
), "master_counts_table as loaded")

```


# Reduction

Most of the table is not expressed: 61% of all genes have a `baseMean_Kelly` of
exactly zero. Expression is therefore the primary filter.

A gene is kept anyway if it has at least 50 publications. That rescue is there so
well-characterised genes stay visible as a reference even when they are silent in
this cell line - TLR2, HFE, NOD2, POSTN and DCN are all annotated HIF targets
that a pure expression cutoff would drop.

**The threshold is deliberately low**, because `pubmed_total` counts *curated
gene-to-publication links*, not mentions. NCBI creates those links mainly for
papers treating a gene as a molecular entity, which systematically undercounts
genes whose literature is old, physiological or biochemical:

| Gene | PubMed full-text search | `pubmed_total` |
|---|---:|---:|
| myoglobin / `MB` | 18,113 | 95 |
| hemoglobin / `HBB` | 286,325 | 876 |
| insulin / `INS` | 522,216 | 1,034 |
| `TP53` | - | 20,399 |

So the column measures how intensively a gene is studied *as a gene*, not how
famous it is. That is usually the more useful reading here - GAPDH scores 637
despite appearing in tens of thousands of papers as a loading control, and those
papers are not about GAPDH - but classic literature is underrepresented, so 50
links already marks a well-studied gene.

One consequence of Ensembl-to-Entrez being many-to-one: 1,691 symbols occupy more
than one row (NLRP2 has four Ensembl loci sharing Entrez 55655), and each row
carries the same literature count. Rows are genes as annotated here, so a count
of "genes above N publications" double-counts those. This comes from the
annotation itself, not from the fallback mapping - the duplication rate is 12.5%
for `annotation` and 13.2% for `symbol_map`.

Literature coverage is used **only** in that direction: it can keep a gene in, it
never throws one out. A strongly expressed but unstudied gene is a candidate, not
noise, and filtering on publication counts would preferentially discard exactly
those - one Kelly-specific target sits at `baseMean` 7,235 with no annotation at
all. `pubmed_total` and `pubmed_hypoxia` otherwise stay in the table as a ranking
aid.

```{r reduction}

min_basemean <- 10
min_pubmed   <- 50

expressed <- !is.na(master$baseMean_Kelly) & master$baseMean_Kelly >= min_basemean
rescued   <- !expressed & !is.na(master$pubmed_total) & master$pubmed_total >= min_pubmed
keep      <- expressed | rescued

dive <- master[keep, ]

# Why each gene is in, so the rescued ones can be excluded again downstream
# without recomputing the rule.
dive$dive_reason <- ifelse(expressed[keep], "expressed", "literature")
dive <- dive %>% dplyr::relocate(dive_reason, .after = symbol)

tab(data.frame(
  Step = c("master_counts_table",
           sprintf("baseMean_Kelly >= %d", min_basemean),
           sprintf("+ rescued: pubmed_total >= %d", min_pubmed)),
  Genes = c(nrow(master), sum(expressed), nrow(dive)),
  Share = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * c(nrow(master), sum(expressed), nrow(dive)) / nrow(master))
), "Reduction")

```

The rescue adds 11% to the table. Worth knowing before using it: 617 of the
rescued genes have a `baseMean` of exactly zero, so they enter as rows of pure
zero counts. That is informative as a reference - "this well-known gene is not
expressed in Kelly" - but they should be excluded from anything that consumes the
count columns, which `dive_reason` makes easy.

```{r rescue_detail, echo=FALSE}

tab(data.frame(
  baseMean = c("exactly 0", "0 - 1", "1 - 10"),
  Genes = c(sum(rescued & master$baseMean_Kelly == 0),
            sum(rescued & master$baseMean_Kelly > 0 & master$baseMean_Kelly < 1),
            sum(rescued & master$baseMean_Kelly >= 1 & master$baseMean_Kelly < min_basemean))
), sprintf("Expression of the %s literature-rescued genes",
           format(sum(rescued), big.mark = ",")))

```

What survives, by annotation. The reduction removes three quarters of the rows
but keeps the large majority of the annotated candidates, which is the point:

```{r reduction_effect, echo=FALSE}

keep_stats <- function(label, sel) {
  data.frame(Set = label,
             before      = sum(sel),
             expressed   = sum(sel & expressed),
             rescued     = sum(sel & rescued),
             after       = sum(sel & keep),
             kept        = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sum(sel & keep) / max(sum(sel), 1)))
}

tab(rbind(
  keep_stats("all genes", rep(TRUE, nrow(master))),
  keep_stats("HIF targets", !is.na(master$Target)),
  keep_stats("Kelly-specific targets",
             !is.na(master$Target) & master$Hx_Baseline == "none" &
               !is.na(master$Hx_Baseline)),
  keep_stats("HR adverse", master$HR_risk == "adverse" & !is.na(master$HR_risk)),
  keep_stats("with hypoxia literature",
             !is.na(master$pubmed_hypoxia) & master$pubmed_hypoxia > 0)
), "Effect of the reduction per annotation set")

```

The best-studied HIF targets that a pure expression cutoff would have dropped -
all of them now retained by the rescue:

```{r rescued_examples, echo=FALSE}

master[rescued & !is.na(master$Target), ] %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(pubmed_total)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(baseMean = round(baseMean_Kelly, 2)) %>%
  dplyr::select(symbol, Target, baseMean, pubmed_total, pubmed_hypoxia) %>%
  head(8) %>%
  tab("HIF targets kept by the literature rescue")

```

Still dropped: annotated targets that are both silent and barely studied. These
are the ones the filter is meant to catch.

```{r dropped_examples, echo=FALSE}

master[!keep & !is.na(master$Target), ] %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(pubmed_total)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(baseMean = round(baseMean_Kelly, 2)) %>%
  dplyr::select(symbol, Target, baseMean, pubmed_total, pubmed_hypoxia) %>%
  head(6) %>%
  tab("Best-studied HIF targets still removed")

```


# Reduced table

```{r dive_preview, echo=FALSE}

dive %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Target), Hx_Baseline == "none", !is.na(symbol)) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.log2FoldChange)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(log2FC = round(Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.log2FoldChange, 2),
                baseMean = round(baseMean_Kelly, 0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(symbol, Target, baseMean, log2FC, HR_risk,
                pubmed_total, pubmed_hypoxia) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  tab("Top Kelly-specific targets in the reduced table")

```

# Risk versus HIF dependence

One panel per HIF, showing every target of that HIF against two axes:

- **x** - clinical risk as `log2(HR)`. Left of zero the gene is protective, right
  of it adverse. The dotted lines mark the 1.5 / 0.67 thresholds used for
  `HR_risk`.
- **y** - HIF dependence, the interaction term negated so that *up* means *more
  dependent on this HIF*. Capped at 8; nine genes sit above it and are drawn at
  the cap.

Two further variables ride along:

| Channel | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Hue | coral / cyan = Kelly-specific, grey = also hypoxic in the baseline lines, pale grey = no baseline data |
| Size and saturation | expression (`baseMean_Kelly`) - one variable on two channels, so faint small dots are lowly expressed and large solid ones are not |

Hues are the genotype colours used elsewhere in the project (`#F8766D` for HIF1A,
`#00BFC4` for HIF2A). The grey had to be lightened to `#D0D0D0`: against a mid
grey the cyan is indistinguishable for red-green colour deficiency (ΔE 2.3), and
at this lightness both hues separate cleanly (ΔE 8.6 and 15.3).

```{r risk_vs_dependence, fig.width=12, fig.height=6.6, dpi=150}

COL <- c("Kelly-specific (HIF1A)" = "#F8766D", "Kelly-specific (HIF2A)" = "#00BFC4",
         "also Hx in SK-N-AS / SH-SY5Y" = "#D0D0D0", "no baseline data" = "#ECECEC")
y_cap <- 8

prep <- function(grp, ycol, panel, tgt_lab) {
  dive %>%
    dplyr::filter(Target %in% grp, !is.na(HR), HR >= 0.1, HR <= 10) %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      panel = panel, symbol,
      log2HR = log2(HR), dep = pmin(-.data[[ycol]], y_cap),
      cls = dplyr::case_when(is.na(Hx_Baseline)     ~ "no baseline data",
                             Hx_Baseline == "none"  ~ tgt_lab,
                             TRUE ~ "also Hx in SK-N-AS / SH-SY5Y"),
      expr = log10(baseMean_Kelly + 1),
      kelly = !is.na(Hx_Baseline) & Hx_Baseline == "none")
}

pdat <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  prep(c("Hif1a", "Hif1a_Hif2a"), "Hif1aHxNx.vs.KellyHxNx.log2FoldChange",
       "HIF1A targets", "Kelly-specific (HIF1A)"),
  prep(c("Hif2a", "Hif1a_Hif2a"), "Hif2aHxNx.vs.KellyHxNx.log2FoldChange",
       "HIF2A targets", "Kelly-specific (HIF2A)"))
pdat$cls   <- factor(pdat$cls, levels = names(COL))
pdat$panel <- factor(pdat$panel, levels = c("HIF1A targets", "HIF2A targets"))

# Label the periphery: the extremes on either axis, whatever category they fall
# into. Those are the genes the plot exists to surface.
edge_labels <- function(d, n_dep = 14, n_hr = 10) {
  d <- d[!is.na(d$symbol), ]
  d[unique(c(head(order(-d$dep), n_dep),
             head(order(-d$log2HR), n_hr),
             head(order(d$log2HR), n_hr))), ]
}
lab <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(split(pdat, pdat$panel), edge_labels))

# Size and alpha both carry expression; identical name/breaks/labels make ggplot
# merge them into a single legend instead of showing the same variable twice.
expr_breaks <- log10(c(10, 1000, 100000) + 1)
expr_labels <- c("10", "1k", "100k")
xr <- range(pdat$log2HR); yr <- range(pdat$dep)

# Each panel only contains three of the four classes, so its colour legend would
# miss a key and the two legends would not be recognised as identical - patchwork
# then stacks both instead of collecting them. This invisible layer carries all
# four levels in every panel, making the legends match exactly.
legend_dummy <- data.frame(log2HR = NA_real_, dep = NA_real_, expr = NA_real_,
                           cls = factor(names(COL), levels = names(COL)))

# The protective / adverse wording is placed at the cutoff coordinates rather than
# used as an axis title, so each word butts against its own threshold line.
hr_line <- log2(1.5)
ann_y   <- yr[1] - 1.2

mk <- function(d, ptitle, show_y) {
  ggplot(d, aes(log2HR, dep)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(-hr_line, hr_line), colour = "black",
               linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.6) +
    # hjust 1 / 0 puts the "|" glyph itself exactly on the cutoff, so it reads as
    # a continuation of the threshold line.
    annotate("text", x = -hr_line, y = ann_y, label = "← protective |",
             hjust = 1, size = 3.1, colour = "grey20") +
    annotate("text", x = hr_line, y = ann_y, label = "| adverse →",
             hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "grey20") +
    geom_point(aes(colour = cls, size = expr, alpha = expr),
               show.legend = c(colour = FALSE, size = TRUE, alpha = TRUE)) +
    geom_point(data = legend_dummy, aes(colour = cls), size = 3.2, alpha = 1,
               na.rm = TRUE) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = dplyr::filter(lab, panel == d$panel[1]),
                             aes(label = symbol), size = 3.2, fontface = "bold",
                             colour = "grey10", box.padding = 0.6,
                             point.padding = 0.2, max.overlaps = Inf,
                             max.time = 2, max.iter = 20000, segment.size = 0.2,
                             segment.colour = "grey55", min.segment.length = 0) +
    # limits = names(COL) keeps the scale identical in both panels, which is what
    # lets patchwork collect the two legends into one.
    scale_colour_manual(values = COL, limits = names(COL), drop = FALSE, name = NULL,
      guide = guide_legend(order = 1, ncol = 1,
                           override.aes = list(size = 3.2, alpha = 1))) +
    scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.8, 5.5), name = "expression (baseMean)",
      breaks = expr_breaks, labels = expr_labels, limits = range(pdat$expr),
      guide = guide_legend(order = 2, ncol = 1, override.aes = list(colour = "grey35"))) +
    scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.35, 1), name = "expression (baseMean)",
      breaks = expr_breaks, labels = expr_labels, limits = range(pdat$expr),
      guide = guide_legend(order = 2, ncol = 1, override.aes = list(colour = "grey35"))) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = xr + c(-0.25, 0.25), ylim = yr + c(-0.15, 0.35),
                    clip = "off") +
    labs(title = ptitle, x = NULL,
         y = if (show_y) sprintf("HIF dependence    −log2FC interaction (capped at %d)",
                                 y_cap) else NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey94"),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
          plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 8, b = 26, l = 5),
          legend.key.height = unit(0.9, "lines"),
          legend.title = element_text(size = 8), legend.text = element_text(size = 8))
}

p1 <- mk(dplyr::filter(pdat, panel == "HIF1A targets"), "HIF1A targets", TRUE)
p2 <- mk(dplyr::filter(pdat, panel == "HIF2A targets"), "HIF2A targets", FALSE)

(p1 + patchwork::guide_area() + p2 +
   patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect", widths = c(1, 0.4, 1))) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(caption = "clinical risk    log2(hazard ratio)") &
  theme(legend.box = "vertical", legend.direction = "vertical",
        legend.justification = "center",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 9.5, colour = "grey25",
                                    margin = margin(t = 4)))

```

```{r plot_counts, echo=FALSE}

n_tot <- function(grp) sum(dive$Target %in% grp)
tab(data.frame(
  Panel = c("HIF1A targets", "HIF2A targets"),
  in_dive = c(n_tot(c("Hif1a", "Hif1a_Hif2a")), n_tot(c("Hif2a", "Hif1a_Hif2a"))),
  plotted = as.integer(table(pdat$panel)),
  Kelly_specific = as.integer(tapply(pdat$kelly, pdat$panel, sum))
), "Genes per panel - the difference to `in_dive` are genes without a usable hazard ratio")

```

# HR Ratio of TOP HIF1A & HIF2A

Hazard ratios for the top HIF1A and HIF2A target genes shown in the HIF-1β
CUT&RUN figure, in the same order and colours. Filled points are significant in
the Cox model (p < 0.05); the dashed lines mark the HR 1.5 / 1/1.5 risk
cutoffs. Two genes carry older symbols in the master table (COXFA4L2 =
NDUFA4L2, CIMAP1B = ODF3L2) and are relabelled here; LINC02649, STEAP1B-AS1
and FRG2B have no survival data.

```{r hr_top_targets, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=6}

top_hif1a <- c("FOXE3", "CA9", "ALOX12B", "DENND1C", "TSPEAR-AS1", "LINC02649",
               "HBD", "ITGB3", "SMIM24", "EXOC3L2", "PFKFB3", "PCP4L1", "CDH15",
               "NDUFA4L2", "ASCL2", "ERVV-1", "PLVAP", "ARRDC2", "GALR1", "CABP7")
top_hif2a <- c("ODF3L2", "IL6R", "FLT1", "EPO", "STEAP1B-AS1", "FRG2B", "CALHM4",
               "KCNK13", "TRAPPC3L", "WT1-AS", "SLC9C2", "SASH1", "THBD",
               "ARHGEF6", "NTSR1", "AGXT", "KLHDC7B", "SLC46A3", "CFAP43",
               "PRODH")
relabel <- c(NDUFA4L2 = "COXFA4L2", ODF3L2 = "CIMAP1B")

hr_top <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    tibble(symbol = top_hif1a, group = "HIF1A targets"),
    tibble(symbol = top_hif2a, group = "HIF2A targets")) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(master %>% dplyr::select(symbol, HR, p_value_HR),
                   by = "symbol") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = ifelse(symbol %in% names(relabel), relabel[symbol], symbol),
    group = factor(group, levels = c("HIF1A targets", "HIF2A targets")),
    sig   = !is.na(p_value_HR) & p_value_HR < 0.05) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(group) %>%
  # Highest HR at the top of each panel; genes without survival data at the bottom.
  dplyr::mutate(label = factor(label, levels = label[order(HR, na.last = FALSE)])) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

hr_cols <- c("HIF1A targets" = "#F8766D", "HIF2A targets" = "#00BFC4")

ggplot(hr_top, aes(y = label, x = HR, colour = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(1/1.5, 1.5), colour = "grey65",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = HR, yend = label),
               linewidth = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = after_scale(ifelse(hr_top$sig, colour, "white"))),
             shape = 21, size = 2.6, stroke = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(data = hr_top %>% dplyr::filter(is.na(HR)),
            aes(x = 1, label = "n/a"), colour = "grey55",
            size = 2.8, hjust = -0.4, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log2",
                     breaks = c(0.5, 1/1.5, 1, 1.5, 2),
                     labels = c("0.5", "0.67", "1", "1.5", "2")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = hr_cols, guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic", colour = "grey15"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey92"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

```


# Hypoxia-induced genes: protective or adverse?

The question, built up in three stages: (1) do the genes that go up under
hypoxia predict better or worse outcome, (2) does the answer differ between
HIF1A and HIF2A targets, and (3) does it depend on the MYCN context - Kelly is
MYCN-amplified, SK-N-AS and SH-SY5Y are not.

Two things to keep in mind when reading the numbers. Only 25,398 of the 64,537
rows have survival data at all (the hazard ratios come from the high-risk
microarray cohort), so every set shrinks once it is intersected with the HR
data. And that background is not 50/50: 23.9% of all genes with survival data
are `adverse` and 18.2% `protective`, so a raw majority is not yet a signal -
each set is therefore also tested *against* that background (Fisher test on
adverse vs protective counts; `OR_adv` > 1 means enriched for adverse).

Sets are defined on the full master table, not the reduced dive table, because
genes induced only in the baseline lines may fail the Kelly expression filter.

```{r hr_polarity_setup}

up_kelly <- !is.na(master$Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.padj) & master$Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.padj < 0.05 &
            master$Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.log2FoldChange > 1
dn_kelly <- !is.na(master$Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.padj) & master$Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.padj < 0.05 &
            master$Kelly.Hx.vs.Nx.log2FoldChange < -1
up_base  <- (!is.na(master$padj_SKNAS)  & master$padj_SKNAS  < 0.05 & master$log2FC_SKNAS  > 1) |
            (!is.na(master$padj_SHSY5Y) & master$padj_SHSY5Y < 0.05 & master$log2FC_SHSY5Y > 1)

has_hr  <- !is.na(master$HR)
bg_adv  <- sum(master$HR_risk == "adverse", na.rm = TRUE)
bg_prot <- sum(master$HR_risk == "protective", na.rm = TRUE)

# One row of statistics per gene set: the within-set majority (binomial test,
# adverse vs protective), the enrichment against the background (Fisher), and
# the continuous shift of the HR distribution (Wilcoxon on log2 HR).
hr_stats <- function(label, stage, sel) {
  s    <- sel & has_hr
  adv  <- sum(master$HR_risk[s] == "adverse")
  prot <- sum(master$HR_risk[s] == "protective")
  fis  <- fisher.test(matrix(c(adv, prot, bg_adv - adv, bg_prot - prot), 2))
  wc   <- wilcox.test(log2(master$HR[s]), log2(master$HR[has_hr & !sel]))
  data.frame(Set = label, stage = stage,
             n = sum(sel), HR_data = sum(s),
             protective = prot, ns = sum(master$HR_risk[s] == "ns"), adverse = adv,
             pct_prot = 100 * prot / sum(s), pct_adv = 100 * adv / sum(s),
             median_HR = median(master$HR[s]),
             p_majority = binom.test(adv, adv + prot)$p.value,
             OR_adv = unname(fis$estimate), p_vs_bg = fis$p.value,
             p_shift = wc$p.value)
}

hr_res <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  hr_stats("Hx up in Kelly",         "Hx in Kelly",  up_kelly),
  hr_stats("Hx down in Kelly",       "Hx in Kelly",  dn_kelly),
  hr_stats("HIF1A targets",          "HIF targets",  master$Target %in% "Hif1a"),
  hr_stats("HIF2A targets",          "HIF targets",  master$Target %in% "Hif2a"),
  hr_stats("HIF1A+HIF2A targets",    "HIF targets",  master$Target %in% "Hif1a_Hif2a"),
  hr_stats("Kelly-specific up",      "MYCN context", up_kelly & !is.na(master$Hx_Baseline) &
                                                       master$Hx_Baseline == "none"),
  hr_stats("up in Kelly + baseline", "MYCN context", up_kelly & !is.na(master$Hx_Baseline) &
                                                       master$Hx_Baseline != "none"),
  hr_stats("baseline-only up",       "MYCN context", up_base & !up_kelly))

hr_tab <- function(stage) {
  hr_res %>%
    dplyr::filter(stage == !!stage) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(pct_prot, pct_adv), ~sprintf("%.1f%%", .x)),
                  median_HR = round(median_HR, 2), OR_adv = round(OR_adv, 2),
                  dplyr::across(c(p_majority, p_vs_bg, p_shift), ~sprintf("%.1e", .x))) %>%
    dplyr::select(-stage)
}

```

## Stage 1: what hypoxia regulates in Kelly

Of the `r format(sum(up_kelly), big.mark = ",")` hypoxia-induced genes,
`r format(hr_res$HR_data[1], big.mark = ",")` have survival data - and among
those, **protective clearly outnumbers adverse** (651 vs 436, binomial
p = 9e-11). Against the adverse-leaning background the depletion is even
stronger (OR 0.47). The mirror image is the more striking result: the genes
hypoxia *represses* are heavily adverse (42% adverse vs 14% protective,
OR 2.5, median HR 1.27). In this cohort the adverse part of the hypoxia
response is what gets switched *off*, not on.

```{r hr_polarity_stage1, echo=FALSE}

tab(hr_tab("Hx in Kelly"), "Hx-regulated genes (Kelly WT, |log2FC| > 1, padj < 0.05) vs survival")

```

## Stage 2: HIF1A vs HIF2A targets

The thesis that HIF1A targets are adverse and HIF2A targets protective is, in
this form, **not supported**: both target sets lean protective, and HIF1A
targets are *not* adverse-enriched (12% adverse vs 15% protective). The direct
comparison of the two ratios is far from significant (Fisher p = 0.40). Only
the continuous view leaves a hint in the expected direction: the HR
distribution of HIF2A targets sits slightly lower (median 0.94 vs 1.00,
Wilcoxon p = 0.013) - a weak protective shift for HIF2A rather than an adverse
shift for HIF1A. The combined HIF1A+HIF2A set is too small to say anything
(5 classified genes).

```{r hr_polarity_stage2, echo=FALSE}

tab(hr_tab("HIF targets"), "HIF target sets (Target column) vs survival")

h1 <- master$Target %in% "Hif1a" & has_hr
h2 <- master$Target %in% "Hif2a" & has_hr
f12 <- fisher.test(matrix(c(sum(master$HR_risk[h1] == "adverse"),
                            sum(master$HR_risk[h1] == "protective"),
                            sum(master$HR_risk[h2] == "adverse"),
                            sum(master$HR_risk[h2] == "protective")), 2))
w12 <- wilcox.test(log2(master$HR[h1]), log2(master$HR[h2]))

tab(data.frame(
  Test = c("adverse:protective ratio, HIF1A vs HIF2A (Fisher)",
           "log2 HR distribution, HIF1A vs HIF2A (Wilcoxon)"),
  p = sprintf("%.2g", c(f12$p.value, w12$p.value))
), "Direct HIF1A vs HIF2A comparison")

```

## Stage 3: the MYCN context

Splitting the hypoxia-induced genes by where they respond: `Hx_Baseline`
separates the Kelly-specific ones (`none`) from those also induced in SK-N-AS /
SH-SY5Y; the third set are genes induced *only* in the baseline lines. The
result is a gradient: the **Kelly-specific response is the most
protective-leaning** (11% adverse, OR 0.38), the shared response sits in the
middle, and the baseline-only response is closest to background - still mildly
protective (OR 0.69, p = 0.017), but with the weakest signal. So the
protective association of hypoxia-induced genes is strongest exactly in the
MYCN-amplified context, and no set flips to adverse.

```{r hr_polarity_stage3, echo=FALSE}

tab(hr_tab("MYCN context"), "Hypoxia-induced genes by cell-line context vs survival")

```

## The whole picture

All eight sets on one axis: share of protective genes to the left, adverse to
the right, with the background shares as dashed reference lines. Every
hypoxia-*induced* set stays left of the background on the adverse side; only
the hypoxia-*repressed* genes break the pattern.

```{r hr_polarity_overview, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}

pol_cols <- c(protective = "#3B6FC9", adverse = "#E8632C")

pol <- hr_res %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Set = factor(Set, levels = rev(Set)),
                stage = factor(stage, levels = unique(stage))) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(pct_prot, pct_adv), names_to = "side", values_to = "pct") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(side = ifelse(side == "pct_prot", "protective", "adverse"),
                x = ifelse(side == "protective", -pct, pct),
                n = ifelse(side == "protective", protective, adverse))

ggplot(pol, aes(x = x, y = Set, fill = side)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.62) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-100 * bg_prot / sum(has_hr), 100 * bg_adv / sum(has_hr)),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n, hjust = ifelse(side == "protective", 1.15, -0.15)),
            size = 2.9, colour = "grey15") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) sprintf("%g%%", abs(x)),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pol_cols, breaks = c("protective", "adverse"),
                    name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(stage ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = "share of genes with survival data (dashed = background)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold", hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "top")

```

**Answer to the opening question:** in these data hypoxia-induced genes are
mainly *protective* - as a raw majority, against the background, and in every
subset tested. The adverse arm of the hypoxia response consists of the genes
hypoxia represses. The HIF1A-adverse / HIF2A-protective split does not hold as
a dichotomy; there is at most a mild protective shift of HIF2A targets. And
the protective lean is strongest in the Kelly-specific (MYCN-amplified)
response. All of this is association in a high-risk cohort, not causality -
adverse-classified single genes still exist in every set (WT1-AS and KLHDC7B
above are examples).
